en: There was no turning back in truth,
You had no deed but probing the gray earth,
There was no time to falter,
His moon-like secret went out across the plain.
Overcome by his majesty,
Ozu burned his people,
Appearing beneath that banner,
He spoke many words of battle,
Truly separating for single combat,
One by one, man against man,
Know that he stretched his path wide as a house,
The head that turned them round,
The pointed head that spun them about,
Roaring loud enough to split ears,
It was a time when Azhy watched,
His fanged body trembled,
In fear his face turned pale,
A word to unite and cast among the people,
A word for all the gathered people,
In wrath he braced his mighty back,
Hero Kenen spoke weighty words,
Speaking of every fear and alarm,
Let me cast fortune upon another,
The battlefield had become harsh,
Let me take them piece by piece.
Having spoken thus, Ozu Khan,
Armored himself in steel beneath the sky,
Striking aside each stone he met,
He devastated the broad Kyrgyz host,
Wearing down the champions,
Burning the great Kyrgyz people,
Scattering sparks like a thrown stone,
Fire flew from his mace,
Venom issued from his storm,
Wrath poured from Ozu Khan,
Upon this unfortunate tribal people,
With the bottomless blue spear,
Devastating them from right and left,
Calling for the house-eagle to come,
He thundered like the sun.
The suffering Kyrgyz, the poor people,
Burned with grief, asking what had happened,
A Kyrgyz man had fallen as a sacrifice,
The dark-faced multitude had bred in abundance,
They said it had drained everything from the multitude,
Seeing the fury, they cried aloud,
“Let us receive it with palms outstretched,”
Let us seek it from the Creator,
Whatever fate may bring, behold it,
I grew accustomed to devastation,
Saying Köböy had taken my honor,
My wrathful, precious soul,
With Ala-Too rising behind you,
For the white-capped Kyrgyz people,
For honor and for the hero,
On the appointed day,
For the livestock that sustains life,
Saying he gave his needed life,
Once gone, he would never return,
Saying he was humbled in this world,
By day and by night,
Across the barren plain where horses ran,
Holding a feast and slaughtering feast-beasts,
Doing a deed that shed radiance,
Kenen stood behind you,
Each of you became a guide,
Calling the tribes Kayyñ, Saryk, and Alay Saryk,
Your people descended into the valley,
At the appointed time a hero came forth,
The two lions came out together,
They cast turmoil into the massed battle,
Does a warrior not die by the enemy?
If he remains mounted in this world,
He closes his eyes and the deed is done,
O enduring multitude of people,
Though spoken, the people here,
To true Köböy, the many people,
Grieved sincerely, saying you had died,
Your true self parted from life,
The closed eyes did not open,
The outstretched legs did not draw back,
Your true soul left your eyes,
Then Kenen truly died,
It became a day of scattering,
The heroes who remained were sorrowful.
Does one destined for death not die?
The albasty took a hundred forms,
Does he not somehow live out his day?
The mark of a lionlike warrior,
While life remained, he did not yield,
Never abandoning a single desire,
Onto the broad field bright as the moon,
As if destined to stand so,
Their thrusting spears clashed,
Without closing their thirsty eyes,
They fought face to face,
The warriors would not retreat from the foe,
The heroes would not leave this world easily,
Would the people’s khan bow his head?
Before this furious Chinese Ozu,
Under this crushing humiliation,
Would a hero consent?
Trusting in his honor and fate,
He drew himself up and stood ready,
Speaking many fateful words,
The land became broad for the dawn riders,
He stood and asked for a blessing,
His coming before Ozu Khan,
Against the Chinese standing in their fortress,
He considered what the enemy would yield,
O noble people of the white-capped Kyrgyz,
Hero Kenen stood in the midst,
A wise man in every hard hour,
Of all wise, plane-tree-like warriors,
He opened his palm and gave his hand,
He gave the firm armor no bullet could pierce,
Forged from blue iron,
For the many battles he had fought,
Worthy of a splendid soul,
They clad him in layer upon layer of iron,
All rose in fury and defiance.
Born as a true thoroughbred,
The term of my splendor ended,
They mounted hero Köböy upon it,
Their hands met and clasped,
The spirits of the forefathers,
Bowed before the Creator,
They covered Köböy in soot,
Köböy rode out to single combat,
Riding toward the furious foe,
The dear heroes received a blessing,
He leveled his battle spear,
A soul born with strength drew near,
To sacrifice himself for the dear people,
All that was within his heart,
He inscribed the writing in blood,
The enraged Ozu Khan,
Dear Köböy was courageous,
Facing humiliation in single combat,
Elder Köböy gave counsel,
The spear champion Köböy,
Had three hundred thousand men,
Köböy’s wisdom was legendary,
He had the finest men,
His champions were exceptional,
His warriors were many,
To the fork-necked Akylska,
To Tarkys, who urged on his horse,
From a haze beyond the reach of sight,
From beyond the distant mirage,
The hero came out onto the battlefield,
Upon the face of the yellow steppe,
Köböy rode forth.
His loud cry became a battle shout,
The hero’s courage rose like spring,
Köböy rode forth,
And Ozu Khan saw him.
And surged forward like a rising flood,
Gripped by fury, he swept in,
Scattering the venom of his rage,
Opening his mouth as if to drive off hunger,
He was a warrior with a gray wolf’s mane,
Wondering what would become of Kögöy,
They prayed that God would prosper his undertaking,
To the Creator, the sole sovereign,
They prayed, “God, protect the warrior,”
The watching people trembled and wailed,
They cried out to him in alarm,
As he plunged among the enemy,
“God, preserve the warrior,” they prayed,
The white-kalpak Kyrgyz cried out together,
“God, grant victory; do not disgrace him,”
The helmet that covered his sight,
Was scraped and battered apart,
His steed came from the broad land,
The bay horse crossed five stretches,
Courageous by his very nature,
The bloody trial came a third time,
My elder Köböy gave counsel,
He parted from the bay horse,
The bay horse fell to a bullet,
He plunged into the mass of the enemy,
Then hero Köböy,
Went on foot, bent nearly double,
True strength came into his soul,
His strength was exhausted in the struggle,
It became a night that blinded the eyes,
If you saw it, it was a grievous day,
His armor hung loose upon him,
Not surrendering to hero Ozu,
The two of us fought,
Who had ever seen such hardship?
Blood flowed from his black eyes,
Dear Köböy stood his ground,
Both hands labored in battle,
A honeyed cry rose to the lips,
The dear youth had strength to stand,
The red vessel filled with blood,
They grappled, bracing with resolve,
They were left bearing regret,
Their strength departed as they struggled,
His dear eyes labored on,
Suffering cruel humiliation,
That accursed, cunning Ozu,
He appeared close upon the battlefield,
Ozu Khan stood in this manner,
One kind among his many forms,
His cunning aspect watched where they settled,
His marksman shot as swiftly as spring.
The majesty of your marksman,
He spread out his back,
Saying the Ayrat deed stood in the midst,
Saying his head and brain were shattered,
Calling the spoil his own,
Your bullet was as large as a sheep’s head,
They bound it in battle and passed on,
They had bound him to true death,
They forced his head to the ground,
Life left him before his face had changed,
Death’s bullet struck his temple,
Our dear elder Köböy,
Had gone to single combat with no other choice.
Seeing this, Ebegey,
Parted from his comrade in sacrifice,
Called the Kyrgyz into the midst,
Broken with grief and separation,
Left diminished and alone,
His soul seared by the loss,
Left solitary like an ascetic,
Without offspring, gathering his remaining strength,
None remained standing; they died,
The figure before them,
Hero Köböy, hard as a hammer,
A warrior-khan to the Kyrgyz,
A close companion beneath one coat,
The people embraced his spreading fame,
Ebegey and Köböy had been born,
Those shared twins,
If a fated bullet struck from above,
Giving a final blessing to the lips,
The enemy could not take the dear hero,
His banner-head stood in the stormy trap,
Nothing remained for those who saw,
Now let me die for his sake.
A lion-hearted soul, truly born,
Created for true honor,
Let me surrender this fly-like life,
Saying this, Ebegey,
Mounted the pale horse of pure milk-color,
Fastening on his coat of mail,
Spurring from right and left,
Casting himself into the countless ranks,
Crying out, “Comrades in sacrifice!”
He attacked hero Ozu,
They fought face to face,
The myriad mouths opened wide,
